work: Ad Arianos (Orationes contra Arianos), Discourse I
ref: Or. 1.14 (NPNF2 section 14; Discourse I, ch. 14)
greek: Οὐ γὰρ ἐκ τινος ἀρχῆς προὐπαρχούσης ὁ Πατὴρ καὶ ὁ Υἱὸς ἐγεννήθησαν, ἵνα καὶ ἀδελφοὶ νομισθῶσιν· ἀλλ᾽ ὁ Πατὴρ ἀρχὴ τοῦ Υἱοῦ καὶ γεννήτωρ ἐστί, καὶ ὁ Πατὴρ πατήρ ἐστι, καὶ οὐχ υἱός τινος γέγονε· καὶ ὁ Υἱὸς δὲ υἱός ἐστι, καὶ οὐχ ἀδελφός. Εἰ δὲ ἀΐδιον γέννημα τοῦ Πατρὸς λέγεται, καλῶς λέγεται.
greek_edition: Migne PG 26 (1857), Athanasius II, via archive.org scan OCR (djvu text). Read from the OCR text (accents and breathings as the OCR gave them; OCR errors possible). Located by matching the English passage; PG column marks in the OCR do not reliably align, so no column is given.
english: For the Father and the Son were not generated from some pre-existing origin, that we may account Them brothers, but the Father is the Origin of the Son and begat Him; and the Father is Father, and not born the Son of any; and the Son is Son, and not brother. Further, if He is called the eternal offspring of the Father, He is rightly so called.
translator: Archibald Robertson (special editor and translator of NPNF2 vol. 4, per the editorial preface)
page: printed p. 824 (PDF p. 854); NPNF2 vol. 4 Four Discourses, ch. 14
edition: Schaff & Wace (eds.), Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers, Second Series vol. 4, New York: Christian Literature Publishing Co., 1892 (CCEL text and PDF cache)
what_it_says: The Son is the Father's eternal offspring, not a brother or a creature, and the Father is never imperfect so that the Son would be added later.
use: supports Trinitarian reading (answers a temporal "begotten at a point" reading by denying any beginning of the generation)
limits: Athanasius does not discuss the endiathetos/prophorikos distinction here, and does not use Theophilus's vocabulary. The Greek is OCR-derived and was read by me, not collated against a second edition.

work: Ad Arianos (Orationes contra Arianos), Discourse I
ref: Or. 1.17 (NPNF2 section 17)
greek: Εἰ γὰρ οὐχ ἀϊδίως σύνεστιν ὁ Λόγος τῷ Πατρὶ, οὐχ ἔστιν ἢ Τριὰς ἀΐδιος· ἀλλὰ μονὰς μὲν ἣν πρότερον, ἐκ προσθήκης δὲ γέγονεν ὕστερον Τριὰς, καὶ προϊόντος τοῦ χρόνου κατ᾽ αὐτοὺς ηὔξησε καὶ συνέστη τῆς θεολογίας ἡ γνῶσις.
greek_edition: Migne PG 26 (1857), Athanasius II, via archive.org scan OCR (djvu text). Read from the OCR text; the OCR shows "ἢ" where the sense requires "ἡ" (possible OCR misprint). Accents as OCR gave them.
english: For if the Word is not with the Father from everlasting, the Triad is not everlasting; but a Monad was first, and afterwards by addition it became a Triad; and so as time went on, it seems what we know concerning God grew and took shape.
page: printed p. 829 (PDF p. 859); NPNF2 vol. 4 Four Discourses, ch. 17
edition: Schaff & Wace (eds.), Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers, Second Series vol. 4, New York: Christian Literature Publishing Co., 1892 (CCEL text and PDF cache)
what_it_says: Athanasius argues that the Triad is eternal only if the Word is eternally with the Father; otherwise the Triad would have been formed by addition.
use: supports Trinitarian reading (the Triad is eternal because the Word is eternal) ; answers the Arian objection that the Son's generation makes the Triad temporal
limits: This is an argument against Arians and does not define the Triad as three persons or hypostases. The word "Triad" here is Athanasius's usage, not evidence about Theophilus, whose use is discussed in U9-08 and U9-09.

work: Ad Arianos (Orationes contra Arianos), Discourse I
ref: Or. 1.18 (NPNF2 section 18)
greek: Οὐχ ἔστι γενητὴ ἡ Τριάς· ἀλλ᾽ ἀΐδιος καὶ μία θεότης ἐστὶν ἐν Τριάδι, καὶ μία δόξα τῆς ἁγίας Τριάδος· καὶ σχίζειν αὐτὴν εἰς διαφόρους φύσεις τολμᾶτε.
greek_edition: Migne PG 26 (1857), Athanasius II, via archive.org scan OCR (djvu text). Read from the OCR text (OCR lines 3383-3387 of the djvu text). Column marker (90) removed.
english: But this is not so: perish the thought; the Triad is not originated; but there is an eternal and one Godhead in a Triad, and there is one Glory of the Holy Triad.
page: printed p. 830 (PDF p. 860); NPNF2 vol. 4 Four Discourses, ch. 18
edition: Schaff & Wace (eds.), Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers, Second Series vol. 4, New York: Christian Literature Publishing Co., 1892 (CCEL text and PDF cache)
what_it_says: The Triad is unoriginated, with one Godhead and one glory in the Triad, against Arian talk of an originated Triad.
use: supports Trinitarian reading (one eternal Godhead in a Triad; one glory of the Holy Triad)
limits: The formula "one Godhead in a Triad" does not spell out how the three are distinct persons. The English "presume to divide it into different natures" is the continuation of the Greek quoted.

work: Ad Arianos (Orationes contra Arianos), Discourse III
ref: Or. 3.67 (NPNF2 section 67)
greek: Οὐχοῦν μὴ λεγέσθω θελήματος δημιούργημα ὁ Υἱὸς, μηδὲ τὰ Οὐαλεντίνου ἐπεισαγέσθω τῇ Ἐκκλησίᾳ, ἀλλὰ βουλὴ ζῶσα, καὶ ἀληθῶς φύσει γέννημα, ὡς τοῦ φωτὸς τὸ ἀπαύγασμα. Οὕτω γὰρ καὶ ὁ μὲν Πατὴρ εἴρηκεν, Ἐξηρεύξατο ἡ καρδία μου Λόγον ἀγαθόν·
greek_edition: Migne PG 26 (1857), Athanasius II, via archive.org scan OCR (djvu text). Read from the OCR text; the OCR line reads "Ἐκ- χλησίᾳ" (hyphen from line break, joined here). Section number is the NPNF/Benedictine section, matched by content.
english: Therefore call not the Son a work of good pleasure; nor bring in the doctrine of Valentinus into the Church; but be He the Living Counsel, and Offspring in truth and nature, as the Radiance from the Light. For thus has the Father spoken, My heart uttered a good Word;
page: printed p. 1065 (PDF p. 1095); NPNF2 vol. 4 Four Discourses, Discourse III, ch. 67
edition: Schaff & Wace (eds.), Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers, Second Series vol. 4, New York: Christian Literature Publishing Co., 1892 (CCEL text and PDF cache)
what_it_says: The Son is not a product of the Father's will but a living Counsel and natural Offspring, like the radiance of light, and the Father "uttered" the Word (Ps. 44/45 LXX).
use: supports Trinitarian reading (the Word is natural, not willed); relevant to the "counsellor" point (living Counsel = the Son)
limits: The "uttered" quotation is the Psalm text, not an analysis of endiathetos/prophorikos. Athanasius treats the Word as Son and Counsel, not a distinct stage of the Word.

work: De Decretis Nicaenae Synodi
ref: De Decr. 21 (NPNF2 section 21)
greek_edition: Greek for this section not located in the OCR (the Psalm 44 phrase found in the OCR belongs to Or. 3.67, see U9-04).
english: For whence may one conceive the Son to be, who is the Wisdom and the Word, in whom all things came to be, but from God Himself? However, the Scriptures also teach us this, since the Father says by David, My heart uttered a good Word, and, From the womb before the morning star I begat Thee
page: printed p. 512 (PDF p. 542); NPNF2 vol. 4 De Decretis section 21
edition: Schaff & Wace (eds.), Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers, Second Series vol. 4, New York: Christian Literature Publishing Co., 1892 (CCEL text and PDF cache)

work: Prolegomena to NPNF2 vol. 4 (editor's introduction, Robertson)
ref: Prolegomena, on the Apologists (Theophilus, Ad Autolycum ii. 10, 22)
greek_edition: English secondary source; no Greek quoted.
english: Before this He was the logos endiathetos, after it the logos prophorikos, the Word uttered (Ps. xlv. 1 LXX; this distinction is not in Justin, but is found Theophil. ad Autol. ii. 10, 22: it is the most marked trace of philosophic [Stoic] influence on the Apologists).
page: printed p. 36 (PDF p. 66); NPNF2 vol. 4 Prolegomena (introductory essay on the Apologists)
edition: Schaff & Wace (eds.), Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers, Second Series vol. 4, New York: Christian Literature Publishing Co., 1892 (CCEL text and PDF cache)
what_it_says: Robertson states that the endiathetos/prophorikos distinction is in Theophilus ad Autolycum ii.10 and 22, and reads it as Stoic influence.
use: objection (a critic can cite this as the Stoic origin of the Word-distinction)
limits: Secondary source, from 1892, and not a reading of Autol. ii.10 or ii.22 by me; it does not say whether Athanasius accepts the distinction.

work: Prolegomena to NPNF2 vol. 4 (editor's introduction, Robertson)
ref: Prolegomena, on Tertullian and the name Trinitas
greek_edition: English secondary source; no Greek quoted.

page: printed p. 37 (PDF p. 67); NPNF2 vol. 4 Prolegomena (Tertullian section)
edition: Schaff & Wace (eds.), Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers, Second Series vol. 4, New York: Christian Literature Publishing Co., 1892 (CCEL text and PDF cache)

work: NPNF2 vol. 4 Prolegomena note on the Triad (footnote, Robertson)
ref: Footnote in the Prolegomena section on Athanasius and the Triad (note on Or. 3 / Benedictine p. 931)
greek_edition: English note quoting Greek word τριὰς only.
english: The word τριὰς, usually translated Trinity, is first used by Theophilus, ad Autol. ii. 15. Gibbon remarks that the doctrine of 'a numerical rather than a generical unity,' which has been explicitly put forth by the Latin Church, is favoured by the Latin language; τριὰς seems to excite the idea of substance, trinitas of qualities.
page: printed p. 520 (PDF p. 550); NPNF2 vol. 4 note on the Triad (keyed to the Benedictine page 931)
edition: Schaff & Wace (eds.), Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers, Second Series vol. 4, New York: Christian Literature Publishing Co., 1892 (CCEL text and PDF cache)
what_it_says: Robertson states that Theophilus, Ad Autolycum ii.15, is the first use of the word triad, and quotes Gibbon on Greek and Latin senses of unity.
use: objection (first-use claim, cited against the Trinitarian reading); also context for the Latin/Greek difference
limits: Secondary; the Gibbon quotation is second-hand. I have not checked Autol. ii.15 itself in this unit.

greek: Ἀρειανοῖς λέγουσι κτίσμα εἶναι τὸ Πνεῦμα τὸ ἅγιον… ἐν μὲν ταῖς Παροιμίαις φανερῶς ἡ Σοφία λέγουσά ἐστι τὸ, «ἔκτισέ με» καὶ ὅμως καλῶς γε ποιοῦντες, ἑρμηνεύετε τὸ ῥητὸν, ἵνα μὴ τὴν δημιουργὸν Σοφίαν ἐν τοῖς κτίσμασι συναριθμῆτε. Τὸ δὲ ἐν τῷ προφήτῃ ῥητὸν οὐκ ἔχει γνώρισμα περὶ τοῦ ἁγίου Πνεύματος, ἀλλ᾽ ἁπλῶς εἴρηται περὶ πνεύματος.
greek_edition: Migne PG 26 (1857), via archive.org OCR, Ad Serapionem I (OCR column marks (89)-(96) near the passage). Greek read from the OCR; ellipsis marks my cut.
english: Own translation (not NPNF): In Proverbs Wisdom plainly says "He created me", and yet you rightly interpret that so that you do not number the Creator Wisdom among the creatures. But the saying in the prophet has no mark that refers it to the Holy Spirit; it simply speaks of "spirit".
translator: Own translation (NPNF2 vol. 4 omits the Ad Serapionem; Shapland 1951 is in copyright and not used)
page: page unknown (PG 26 columns about 88-96 by OCR marks)
edition: Migne PG 26 (1857), Athanasius II, via archive.org scan OCR (djvu text)

limits: Own translation. Only the Greek is quoted from a source; the section number is not reliable from the OCR. The Ad Serapionem is not in the NPNF2 volume, so no published English was verified.

work: Commentary on John (In Joannem), Book I
ref: Comm. Jo. 1.22 (Menzies section 22)
greek: Κατὰ τοῦτο δὲ τὸ ὡς γενέσεως σημαινόμενον τὴν ἀρχὴν, καὶ τὸ ὑπὸ τῆς σοφίας ἐν Παροιμίαις λεγόμενον ἐκδέξασθαι δυνησόμεθα· Ὁ Θεὸς γὰρ, φησὶν, ἔκτισέ με ἀρχὴν ὁδῶν αὐτοῦ εἰς ἔργα αὐτοῦ.
greek_edition: Migne PG 14 (1857), via archive.org OCR (patrologiae_cursus_completus_gr_vol_014). Located by matching the English section (Proverbs 8:22 quotation near "arche"); PG column not confirmed.
english: But Christ is demiurge as a beginning (arche), inasmuch as He is wisdom. It is in virtue of His being wisdom that He is called arche. For Wisdom says in Solomon: God created me the beginning of His ways, for His works, so that the Word might be in an arche, namely, in wisdom.
translator: Allan Menzies (Ante-Nicene Fathers vol. 9, 1896; as posted on newadvent)
page: page unknown
edition: Ante-Nicene Fathers vol. 9 (Menzies, Buffalo 1896) via newadvent
what_it_says: Origen says the Word is the beginning (arche) because He is Wisdom, and reads Prov. 8:22 of the Word-in-Wisdom.
use: supports Trinitarian reading (Word and Wisdom are one Son, prior to creation); bears on the arche point (item 4 of the brief)
limits: Origen here is not a Nicene text and uses "Wisdom" and "Word" as titles of Christ in his own scheme; the Greek match is by content, so it needs a column check. I did not find the word "Triad" in Book I (searched the Menzies text).

work: Adversus haereses (Against Heresies), Book IV

limits: This is an editorial summary, not a primary Hilary text; I did not verify the primary De Trinitate passages (see notes.md).

work: Nicene Creed as quoted in De Decretis (Greek, OCR)
ref: Creed of Nicaea (the text quoted by Athanasius in De Decretis, the "Faith dictated in the Council")
greek: Εἰς τὸν ἕνα Κύριον Ἰησοῦν Χριστὸν, τὸν Υἱὸν τοῦ Θεοῦ, γεννηθέντα ἐκ τοῦ Πατρὸς μονογενῆ, τουτέστιν ἐκ τῆς οὐσίας τοῦ Πατρὸς, Θεὸν ἐκ θεοῦ, φῶς ἐκ φωτὸς, Θεὸν ἀληθινὸν ἐκ Θεοῦ ἀληθινοῦ, γεννηθέντα, οὐ ποιηθέντα, ὁμοούσιον τῷ Πατρὶ, δι᾽ οὗ τὰ πάντα ἐγένετο.
greek_edition: Migne PG 26 (1857), Athanasius II, via archive.org scan OCR (djvu text). OCR line reads "οὔ Θεοῦ" where τοῦ Θεοῦ is meant (corrected here); the column marker (94) removed.
english: And in One Lord Jesus Christ, the Son of God, begotten of the Father, Only-begotten, that is, from the essence of the Father; God from God, Light from Light, Very God from Very God, begotten not made, One in essence with the Father, by Whom all things were made
page: printed p. 346 (PDF p. 376); NPNF2 vol. 4, "The Faith dictated in the Council"
edition: Schaff & Wace (eds.), Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers, Second Series vol. 4, New York: Christian Literature Publishing Co., 1892 (CCEL text and PDF cache)
what_it_says: The creed says the Son is begotten, not made, of the essence of the Father, and one in essence (homoousios) with the Father.
use: supports Trinitarian reading (begotten not made; homoousios)
limits: Greek from OCR; the creed text is the Council's formula as quoted by Athanasius (not the 381 creed). The "one in essence" phrase is the disputed term Athanasius defends (see De Decr. 20-24, U9-05/06).

work: Creeds of Christendom (Schaff), Latin Western form
ref: Forma Recepta, Ecclesiae Occidentalis (Nicene Creed, Latin)
greek_edition: Latin text as printed by Schaff.
english: Et in unum Dominum Jesum Christum, Filium Dei [unigenitum], natum ex Patre ante omnia saecula [Lumen de Lumine], Deum verum de Deo vero, natum [genitum], non factum, consubstantialem Patri; per quem omnia facta sunt. (Latin, quoted; no English translation of this line is claimed here.)
translator: Latin text, Schaff (Creeds of Christendom, vol. 2); no translator
page: printed p. 84 (PDF p. 91); Schaff, Creeds of Christendom vol. 2, "Forma Recepta"
edition: Schaff, Creeds of Christendom, vol. 2 (CCEL cache)
what_it_says: The Western form of the Nicene Creed has the Son natum, non factum, consubstantialem Patri.
use: supports Trinitarian reading (begotten, not made; consubstantial)
limits: The English column in the schema is left as the Latin quotation; the Latin bracketed words are Schaff's apparatus, not the creed.
